turns.user: Explain closed-loop handoffs for our software support team, with a practical example.
turns.assistant:
A closed-loop handoff means work changes hands only after the receiver understands the next step and explicitly accepts responsibility. Sending a ticket or tagging someone isn’t enough.

Use four steps:
1. State the status: what’s happening, what you’ve tried, and what remains open.
2. Explain the next action, deadline, dependencies, warning signs, and escalation contact.
3. Ask the receiver to restate the critical action. Correct any gaps.
4. Confirm acceptance and record who now owns the work.

Practical example: a support ticket crossing shifts

Outgoing agent:
“Ticket #482 concerns intermittent login failures for one customer. We’ve reproduced the issue and attached logs; engineering is investigating. The customer’s next update is due at 3 p.m., even if there’s no fix. Check the engineering thread at 2:30. If failures spread to other customers, escalate to the incident lead. Can you take ownership?”

Incoming agent:
“I’ll check engineering at 2:30 and update the customer by 3 regardless of progress. If other customers are affected, I’ll contact the incident lead. I’ve reviewed the ticket and can take ownership.”

Outgoing agent:
“Correct. I’ve recorded you as the owner, with those next steps.”

The handoff is complete; the customer issue is still open.

Practical limit: acceptance requires capacity, access, and authority. If the receiver can’t take it, the sender retains ownership or uses the established escalation route until an appropriate person accepts. A completed checklist doesn’t fix understaffing.

[Closed-loop handoff guide](https://github.com/haitaowu12/leadership-toolbox/blob/main/skills/leadership-toolbox/references/methods/L14-handoff.md#try-it)

turns.user: Can I say this will reduce our incidents by 23%?
turns.assistant:
No. That would overstate what the evidence supports.

The roughly 23% figure comes from a study of the multicomponent I-PASS handoff program across nine pediatric training programs: medical errors fell from 24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions. It was a nonrandomized before-and-after study, and it didn’t isolate closed-loop confirmation from the rest of the program. It cannot predict a 23% reduction in your software incidents. [Starmer et al., 2014](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1405556)

For a proposal, you could say:
“Closed-loop handoffs make ownership and next steps explicit. We propose testing whether they reduce missed actions and handoff-related incidents in our support team; the size of any improvement is currently unknown.”

If you mention 23%, label it as the observed medical-error reduction in that clinical program, not an expected result for your team.

turns.user: People stay silent in meetings. The last person who disagreed says their manager threatened their job. Should I run 1-2-4-All?
turns.assistant:
No, not while that threat is unresolved. The report of a job threat creates a credible retaliation concern. 1-2-4-All gives people turns but cannot protect them from consequences of speaking.

Pause the exercise and use an established route outside the implicated manager’s control, such as an independent ombuds or appropriate HR/ethics contact, to arrange protection and qualified handling. Don’t ask the team to air the allegation or promise anonymity or confidentiality you cannot guarantee.

Privately, you could say: “Thank you for telling me. I take this seriously. Before you share more, let’s clarify who may need to know and what options exist to protect you.”

Reconsider participation exercises only when credible protection is in place and participation is voluntary.
